participants were able to describe their own eating behaviors, but not to connect this with self-kindness.
participants did not associate self-kindness with eating or other health behaviors, but did engage in eating, exercise and other health practices as a form of self-regulation.
the participants' narratives were dominated by the concept of self-control in relation to eating and exercise behaviors, and self-care and kindness were not associated with health behaviors.

how people understand and experience self-kindness and how it relates to eating and other health behaviors.
the experiences of self-kindness in eating behaviors, and the implications for the development of mindfulness-based eating interventions.
the experience of eating behaviors and the understanding of self-care, and the relationship between self-kindness and health behaviors, and the implications for mindfulness-based interventions.

there is an absence of a coherent and integrated concept of self-kindness within a context of eating, weight regulation and other health behaviors.
the participants in this study described eating behaviors and self-kindness in ways that are at odds with the current literature and the current conceptualizations of mindfulness and mindful eating.
the concept of self-kindness in the context of eating and health behaviors is not yet well understood, nor is it widely accepted as a way to enhance health behaviors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
self-kindness is a difficult construct to relate to eating behaviors, particularly in the context of health and wellbeing.
participants in this study were able to describe a range of eating and health behaviors that were not associated with the notion of kindness to oneself.
the participants described a number of different approaches to eating and health behaviors.

self-kindness is a concept which is poorly understood by participants and is associated with negative connotations of being self-indulgent and selfish.
